title: Tu Hai Meri Kiran Review: A Clever Time-Phone Premise the Second Half Cannot Carry
excerpt: Sonakshi Sinha and Zaheer Iqbal lead Karan Rawal's Hindi thriller about a phone that connects 2026 to 2016. Critics praise the idea and the performances, then fault the convoluted payoff.
body:
• Tu Hai Meri Kiran, a Hindi-language romance thriller directed by Karan Rawal and starring Sonakshi Sinha and Zaheer Iqbal, released in theatres on October 23, 2026.
  • Critics agree on the hook: a mysterious feature phone connects author Kiran in 2026 with Samar in 2016, and his fascination turns into stalking — an intriguing premise with an engaging, twist-filled first half.
  • The verdicts diverge after the interval: Bollywood Hungama rated it 2.5/5 and India Forums 2/5, both faulting a convoluted second half, unanswered questions about the phone, and a climax that does not land.
  • Performances are the consensus strength — Sinha is convincing as Kiran and Iqbal is unsettling as Samar — but the film opened in a crowded pre-Diwali frame and, per early box-office reporting, faces an uphill run.

Tu Hai Meri Kiran is a Hindi-language romance thriller written and directed by Karan Rawal, released in theatres on October 23, 2026. Sonakshi Sinha plays Kiran Mittal, a bestselling author blocked on her next book, and Zaheer Iqbal plays Samar, the man whose interest in her curdles into obsession. The twist, which arrives in the first 15 minutes, is that the two are connected across time by a mysterious feature phone — she is in 2026, he is in 2016 — and that advantage gives Samar a dangerous hold over her life.

The Setup

Kiran lives in a hilly region with her husband Riyaan Malhotra (Ankit Gupta). She suspects Riyaan of cheating, her relationship with her father Mahesh Mittal (Purnendu Bhattacharya) is strained, and into that unsettled life walks Samar. Filmfare notes the title's deliberate echo of Darr (1993), Yash Chopra's obsessive-lover thriller, and argues Rawal's paranormal angle is what separates this film from that template: distance and time do not protect Kiran, because the phone lets Samar intrude anyway. The supporting cast includes Zarina Wahab as Samar's mother Seema and Sherlin Seth as Sakshi.

The Consensus

The consensus: Three early published reviews — Bollywood Hungama (2.5/5), India Forums (2/5) and Filmfare — land in the same place: a genuinely fresh premise and a gripping first half, undone by a second half that piles on twists without explaining its own rules. The rated reviews average just above 2 out of 5.

What's praised: The unpredictability of the first half — Hungama says the developments are so novel that "one is unable to predict what will happen next" — and the two leads. Sinha is described as aptly cast and convincing, charting Kiran's shift from distress to resolve, while Iqbal slips between Samar's innocent surface and his menace. Technically, Atanu Mukherjee's editing is praised for the transitions between the two timelines, Utkarsh Marulkar's cinematography is called appropriate, and the single song, "Na Roko," plus the background score by Advait Nemlekar and Shalom Benjamin, support the drama.

What's criticized: The phone itself. No review found an explanation for why the device connects two timelines, and India Forums argues the film behaves "as though the concept itself should do all the storytelling," leaving the rules of the connection, and how changing 2016 alters 2026, unanswered. The second half draws the sharpest fire: developments become hard to digest, character decisions serve the plot, the climax feels like an escape route rather than a conclusion, and supporting tracks — Riyaan's marriage, the father's estrangement — stay underwritten.

"The phone may connect two timelines, but it cannot connect the dots the writers leave behind."

— India Forums review of Tu Hai Meri Kiran

Film Details and What This Means for You

The film runs 2 hours 5 minutes, carries a U/A certificate, and comes from Echelon Productions, PAM Studio and AND Productions, per Bollywood Hungama's cast and crew listing. It is a theatrical release; no streaming date has been announced in the coverage reviewed.

What this means for you: For diaspora viewers, this is a wait-for-streaming proposition unless the premise alone hooks you. Thriller fans who enjoy a high-concept first hour will find the opening genuinely absorbing, and Iqbal's performance is a step up. But if you need a mystery to pay off its own setup, the consensus says this one does not — and it opened in a crowded, dull pre-Diwali frame that Hungama expects will make its theatrical run harder still.

data_cards.rating_consensus: Across three early published reviews, critics praise the time-crossed phone premise, the unpredictable first half and the lead performances, and fault a convoluted second half, unexplained rules for the device, and a climax that does not resolve the setup. The two rated reviews — Bollywood Hungama at 2.5/5 and India Forums at 2/5 — average just above 2 out of 5; The Videshi rates it 2.5/5 on the strength of its first half and performances.
